source: Greiner, Smith, Wilkerson (1989) A correction to the algorithm in Reiter's theory of diagnosis
finding: Reiter's pruned breadth-first HS-tree can lose minimal hitting sets. The bug comes from two rules interacting: the rule that closes a node whose label set was already used, and the rule that removes redundant edges when a subset conflict appears.
numbers: Counterexample collection {{a,b},{b,c},{a,c},{b,d},{b}}: the pruned tree no longer represents the minimal hitting set {a,b}. A second case {{a,b},{a},{b}} shows why node relabeling is needed. Paper is 10 pages, no benchmark.
quote: it is the application of a technique for handling the non-minimal conflict sets that introduces a bug
limits: Bug only appears when conflict sets are non-minimal (the theorem prover returns a superset of an earlier conflict). With only minimal conflicts, the original tree is fine.
agent_relevance: Any search over suspects that prunes by an early-found small set can silently drop valid answers when later evidence shrinks a conflict. Keep a rule to revisit pruned branches.

source: Greiner, Smith, Wilkerson (1989) HS-DAG repair
finding: The fix is HS-DAG: a directed acyclic graph instead of a tree. Nodes are reused when the same path set recurs. When a smaller conflict is found, the old label is replaced and now-redundant edges are removed. The paper proves correctness (Theorem 2) and that pruning yields the DAG for some reordering of the collection.
numbers: Theorem 2 (correctness of hs-dag); Figures 3 and 4 show a partial DAG and its pruned form. No runtime numbers.
limits: Proof only; no empirical test. Cost of relabeling and subset checks is not analysed.
agent_relevance: Search state should be a graph of suspect sets with reuse, not a tree that forgets. Relabel nodes when a conflict shrinks.

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles (as restated in Greiner et al. 1989)
finding: Diagnoses are exactly the minimal hitting sets of the conflict sets (Reiter's Theorem 4.4). The HS-tree builds them breadth-first with pruning rules: close on a duplicate or subset label, and remove redundant edges.
numbers: Theorem 4.4 as restated in Greiner et al.; the original paper was not opened this session.
limits: Second-hand reading through Greiner et al. and Rodler (2019). Reiter treats conflict computation by a theorem prover as the expensive step.
agent_relevance: The theory gives the scaffold a clean rule: suspects to test are the minimal sets that hit all conflicts found so far.

source: Landscape survey (2016) The minimal hitting set generation problem: algorithms and computation
finding: The survey says Greiner et al. showed Reiter's algorithm to be incomplete, and that the repair gives up acyclicity (HS-DAG). Wotawa (2001) later adjusted the algorithm to need fewer containment checks, which makes the DAG unnecessary, giving the tree variant HST.
numbers: No formal complexity analysis of HS-DAG or HST is known to the authors. Both can search bounded cardinality by limiting depth.
limits: A survey claim; the opened text does not show HS-DAG or HST in its benchmark tables.
agent_relevance: A bounded-depth search is a ready control knob: cap suspect-set size for a cheap first pass.

source: Wotawa (2001) A variant of Reiter's hitting-set algorithm, Information Processing Letters 79(1)
finding: Reported second-hand: a variant that avoids the DAG by cutting containment checks, restoring a plain tree with the same output.
numbers: Not opened; described in the 2016 survey and in Pill et al. 2016.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Shows the DAG was a cost of one pruning method, not essential to the idea.

source: Survey benchmark (2016) of about two dozen minimal hitting set algorithms
finding: Large comparison on inputs derived from real data. The tree/DAG diagnosis algorithms are not the fastest: MMCS, RS and HTC-BDD are far faster across inputs.
numbers: Time limit 3600 s; medians over 3 runs; cutoff sizes c=5,7,10; 1 to 16 threads on 8 cores, 32 GB. HTC-BDD beats its closest rival by 4 to 10 times on many inputs but often runs out of memory. Parallel MHS2 shows a 2.33x gain. One input has about 500 sets and about 128 million minimal hitting sets.
limits: Inputs came from data mining and biology, not diagnosis. The authors warn implementations vary hugely, so benchmark on your own data.
agent_relevance: Raw enumeration speed is not the issue for an LLM scaffold; the sets are tiny. What matters is bounded size and conflict quality.

source: Pill, Quaritsch, Wotawa (2016) On the practical performance of minimal hitting set algorithms from a diagnostic perspective
finding: Head-to-head test of complete minimal hitting set algorithms on synthetic and ISCAS circuit data. The Boolean algorithm and GDE's method are the top performers. HS-DAG and HST are mid-pack. SAT-based hitting set solvers are the slowest.
numbers: Limits 300 s and 2 GiB. Four real scenarios TSR1-4 with 202 to 880 components, 100 samples each. SAT variants were on average about two orders of magnitude slower than HS-DAG, HST and GDE.
limits: Pre-computed conflict sets were given, so the test isolates the hitting step. Single laptop. The authors say ranking depends on problem size and cardinality bound.
agent_relevance: The simple method wins on small inputs. A small agent-side suspect search does not need heavy machinery.

source: Pill et al. (2016) size-dependent ranking on artificial scenarios TSA1 and TSA2
finding: Ranking flips with size. GDE beats all methods up to run times of 10 ms (about 30 components). The Boolean algorithms then take the lead and beat GDE by more than 10x beyond 200 components. HS-DAG catches up near 500 ms run times.
numbers: Averages of 20 samples, 100 components, max hitting set size 3. Boolean-iterative used almost two orders of magnitude more memory than the best at 4000 conflict sets; without its optimisations the Boolean crossover fell from about 500 to about 20 sets.
limits: Artificial data (disjoint or random conflict sets). The Boolean ranking moved between TSA1 (worse at small sizes) and TSA2 (worse at large sizes), so there is no single trend.
agent_relevance: No universal best search order; choose cheap and simple for small suspect sets.

source: Pill et al. (2016) HS-DAG versus HST, and complete Staccato
finding: HST usually beats HS-DAG when only single-element hitting sets are wanted, but HS-DAG wins most of the range when sets of size up to 3 are wanted. Staccato, run in complete mode, was very slow and could not even solve the smallest TSA2 samples.
numbers: Max size 1 and 2: HST ahead most of the time. Max size 3: HS-DAG ahead for the majority of the range, HST ahead for smaller problems. GDE and recursive Boolean were the only methods finishing all samples with no resource violation at size 3.
limits: Result depends on implementation and cardinality bound; the Wotawa fix does not dominate the Greiner DAG.
agent_relevance: The DAG-versus-tree choice is a modest constant factor; the correctness of reuse matters more than speed.

source: Pill et al. (2016) why keep HS-DAG and HST
finding: The authors keep HS-DAG and HST because they can drive on-the-fly conflict computation: test whether the components in a node are faulty, and if not, ask a solver for an unsatisfiable core as the next node label. The faster methods need all conflicts first.
numbers: Their ISCAS conflict sets were themselves produced by a cardinality-restricted HS-DAG run using the Yices prover.
limits: Qualitative argument from the Discussion section.
agent_relevance: This lazy conflict-then-hit loop is the shape of an LLM-guided search: each node asks the model or a checker for one fresh conflict.

source: Metodi, Stern, Kalech, Codish (2014) A novel SAT-based approach to model based diagnosis, JAIR 51
finding: A direct SAT encoding (SATbD) finds minimum-cardinality diagnoses far faster than earlier complete searches (HA*, CDA*). It is the main rival to the conflict-then-hit paradigm.
numbers: c7552 system, 1557 observations: 99.3% solved in 30 s (11 unsolved), all solved within 80 s. In the extra-statistics table CDA* finds no minimal-cardinality diagnosis at all from c1355 upward. SAFARI returned a true minimum-cardinality diagnosis in only 13% of cases at 80 s, with answers 1.68x too large on average.
limits: Author-run comparison on ISCAS-85 and 74XXX circuits with 30 s timeouts. HS-DAG itself was not the baseline.
agent_relevance: For well-formed logic problems a direct solver beats suspect-tree search. An agent should call a solver where one exists.

source: Metodi et al. (2014) all-minimal-cardinality comparison
finding: For finding all minimal cardinality diagnoses, SATbD is faster by orders of magnitude on larger systems than HDIAG and DCAS.
numbers: Siddiqi observation set, cardinality bounded by 8, 1800 s timeout.
limits: HDIAG and DCAS numbers were copied from Siddiqi and Huang (2011), run on a different machine, with an advantage for SATbD.
agent_relevance: Cross-machine speed claims need a discount.

source: Rodler (2022) Sound, complete, linear-space, best-first diagnosis search (RBF-HS)
finding: RBF-HS replaces the stored open list of HS-Tree with recursive best-first search, keeping soundness, completeness and best-first order. It saves large amounts of memory and is often not slower.
numbers: Real knowledge-base debugging cases; min/avg/max runtime 0.04/24/744 s and 9/17.5K/1.3M tree nodes. Memory saving up to 98%; HS-Tree used up to 4900% more memory. In 40% of cases RBF-HS had equal or lower runtime, with time savings up to more than 88%. Parameter ld in {2,6,10,20}.
limits: Minimum-cardinality task only. On trivial problems the trade is not favourable; the gain grows with size. Own-lab benchmark.
agent_relevance: Linear-space best-first search over suspects keeps scaffold memory bounded, which matches a limited context.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: hardness remark
finding: Even with a polynomial theorem prover, computing one more minimal diagnosis given a non-empty set of minimal diagnoses is NP-hard. HS-Tree needs exponential space because all open paths are stored for best-first order.
numbers: Footnote 1 and introduction; ontology debugging cited as 2-NEXPTIME-complete for some logics.
limits: Worst case; the real cases in the study stayed under 1.3M nodes.
agent_relevance: Never promise a complete enumeration; plan to sample the best few suspects.

source: Rodler (2019) Towards optimizing Reiter's HS-Tree for sequential diagnosis (preliminary DynamicHS)
finding: Standard practice discards the whole tree after each new measurement, though most of it is still valid. DynamicHS keeps and repairs the tree. Reiter himself asked in 1987 whether new diagnoses can be built from the old tree; the paper says no algorithm answered this before.
numbers: First results on real knowledge bases (ld=6, random fault probabilities): 59% fewer expensive reasoner calls and 42% less time on average; less time in every observed session.
quote: When new diagnoses do arise as a result of system measurements, can we determine these new diagnoses in a reasonable way
limits: Workshop paper, preliminary results only.
agent_relevance: Keep conflicts across turns. Do not throw away evidence when a new observation arrives.

source: Rodler (2021) DynamicHS: streamlining Reiter's HS-Tree for sequential diagnosis (full evaluation)
finding: The full study confirms the preliminary result at larger scale. DynamicHS gives the same solutions as HS-Tree and is faster in nearly all runs. The saving does not depend on the number of diagnoses asked for or on the measurement-selection heuristic.
numbers: Faster in 99.4% of scenarios and 96% of single sessions; per heuristic ENT 96%, SPL 97%, MPS 95%. Median saving 52%, maximum 75%; HS-Tree up to 4x slower on average, over 9x in single sessions. Hardest cases per scenario: median 64%, max 89%. 20 sessions per scenario, ld in {2,4,6,10,20,30}, Pellet reasoner, QuickXPlain for conflicts.
limits: Description-logic knowledge-base debugging only. Trades space for time (state is kept).
agent_relevance: Reusing prior conflicts is the best-supported speed-up in this literature; map it to a conflict store carried across steps.

source: Rodler (2021) DynamicHS: where it loses
finding: There are small failures. Median runtime was slightly worse in two scenarios, and in two single scenarios HS-Tree needed much less time. Absolute losses were small.
numbers: Median losses of 2% for (SPL, D, 30) and 3% for (MPS, fal-ce, 30). In extreme scenarios HS-Tree took 76% (ctx-se, 20) and 32% (D, 30) less time. DynamicHS never needed more than 0.8 s more (first case) or 12 s more (second) in any of the 20 runs.
limits: Fault probabilities were chosen uniformly at random, which may not match real use.
agent_relevance: Boundary: state reuse costs space and some overhead; for tiny trees, rebuilding is fine.

source: Shchekotykhin, Jannach, Schmitz (2015) MergeXplain: fast computation of multiple conflicts for diagnosis (IJCAI)
finding: Producing several conflicts per prover call, by divide and conquer, cuts total diagnosis time. QuickXplain (QXP) returns one conflict per call and restarts at each new HS-tree node.
numbers: DXC 2011 synthetic benchmark, 20 fault scenarios per system: gain 15% to 45% for the first 5 diagnoses. CSP and spreadsheet cases: up to 54%. Simulated conflict positions: 20-30% in the random case, up to 75% when conflicts are placed unfavourably for QXP. Averages of 100 runs, shuffled constraint order.
limits: When only one conflict exists, MXP slightly loses (queens-8 -11%, revenue calculation -5%). Hard problems benefit most. Laptop, Java framework, Choco solver.
agent_relevance: Ask for many candidate conflicts per model call, not one, and let the search merge them.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) Are diagnostic concepts within the reach of LLMs? (DX 2025)
finding: First test I found that asks LLMs to run the conflict then minimal-diagnosis pipeline on circuits. Reasoning models do surprisingly well on conflicts and less well on the hitting-set step. The authors still say LLMs are no alternative to diagnosis algorithms.
numbers: 23 arithmetic and logic circuits. o3-mini: F1 = 0.917 +/- 0.249 for conflicts, 0.784 +/- 0.322 for diagnoses. o1 best on conflicts; o3-mini best on diagnoses. Up to 165 minimal diagnoses per example. 10 repeats for 4o-mini and o3-mini, one run for o1.
limits: Small systems; every step got correct inputs from the gold pipeline, so real chained error would be worse. All inputs and outputs assumed measured; component faults only.
agent_relevance: Treat model-made conflicts as good but unverified; compute the hitting set with code, not in the head.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) design and weak points
finding: Diagnosis generation is the most compute-heavy step and declines clearly as the number of diagnoses and relations grows. Non-reasoning models fail badly: gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini had accuracy close to zero on unseen examples without a code interpreter. 4o-mini added known variables and faults to the incidence matrix.
numbers: Diagnosis prompt contained pseudo-code of the algorithm and a worked example. o1 and o3-mini got perfect incidence matrices. One o1 iteration cost about 30 USD. Reasoning effort high (dedicated) or medium (broad).
limits: The hitting-set work was given as pseudo-code in the prompt, not as a tree search, and tree search was not measured. One lab, one model family (OpenAI).
agent_relevance: The hitting-set step degrades with answer count; do not ask the model for all diagnoses at once.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) Using SLMs and LLMs for diagnosis (DX 2026)
finding: Thirteen language models were asked to diagnose electric circuits and heating systems from a text description. Bigger models were better, but even the best hallucinated in about one answer in five.
numbers: 7 systems, 13 models (10 small, 3 larger). Hit rate: Gemini 2.5 Flash 79.5%, Mistral Large 76.9%, Llama 4 Scout 17B 38.5%, Mistral 7B 25.6%, Phi-2 and TinyLlama 0%. Hallucination rate 20.5%, 15.4%, 7.7% for the top three; most small models above 70%; Llama 3.2 1B 94.9%. Rank-sum ranking agreed with the weighted ranking for all 13.
limits: Small systems, manual scoring by the authors (possible bias), only freely available models, no hitting-set method, no tree search. Heating systems were harder than circuits.
agent_relevance: Without a structured search, models name plausible but wrong faults; a suspect-search scaffold aims to curb that.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) scoring and multiple-fault handling
finding: The score weights correctness 30%, reasoning 20%, hallucination 20%, completeness 15%, uncertainty 10%, clarity 5%. A response earns top uncertainty credit when it admits several fault candidates are possible; naming one fault without justification when several are present scores low.
numbers: The largest gap between top and bottom models is in correctness and completeness; clarity is the strongest category for all. Mean standard deviation under 0.47 for the top three versus above 0.6 for most small models.
limits: Hand-defined weights; author-scored.
agent_relevance: Reward listing alternative suspects, which is what a hitting-set frontier holds.

source: Zhang, Chen, Chen (2026) Satisfiability solving with LLMs: a matched-pair evaluation (FSE 2026)
finding: Checking whether constraints conflict (UNSAT) is the weak side for LLMs. Most models label nearly every formula satisfiable, miss the easy-hard-easy phase transition, and fall as variables grow. Only reasoning models (GPT-5, o1, DeepSeek-reasoner) hold up.
numbers: More than 2700 3-SAT formulas and over 700 2-SAT formulas; reasoning models reach very high paired accuracy (ADR) on 2-SAT even above 50 variables; answers on CNF and on Vertex Cover or 3D-packing versions agree on more than 80% of instances. Plain accuracy and F1 were misleading.
limits: Not diagnosis. A conflict is an UNSAT core, so this is only a proxy for conflict detection.
agent_relevance: A model that says everything is consistent will never produce conflicts to hit; test conflict detection on matched pairs.

source: Xu, Liu et al. (2026) Delta-1 plus LLM: symbolic-neural integration for explainable reasoning
finding: A theorem generator builds minimal unsatisfiable clause sets and an LLM only verbalises them. The paper notes that MARCO and MUSer2 enumerate minimal unsatisfiable subsets by hitting-set dualization.
numbers: No benchmark numbers; case studies in health care, compliance and contract analysis.
limits: Weak evidence: demonstrations only; the LLM does not search.
agent_relevance: Splitting the work (symbolic core finds minimal sets, model explains) is a pattern, but unmeasured here.

source: Grastien, Haslum, Thiebaux (2023) A more general theory of diagnosis from first principles
finding: Found by search only: generalises Reiter's framework beyond static systems. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers collected.
limits: Search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Background for dynamic systems; not used.

source: AgentLocate (2026) Who broke the system? Failure localization in LLM-based multi-agent systems (COLM 2026)
finding: Search snippet only: blames a responsible agent and earliest decisive step with LLM judging, multi-view verification and confidence-aware aggregation. Not a hitting-set method.
numbers: No numbers collected.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Related blame-search task; treat as unverified.

source: TU Delft thesis (2026) Fault localization in LLM-based multi-agent systems, scope-guided judging
finding: Search snippet only: scope guidance does not generally help over judging the whole trace.
numbers: No numbers collected.
limits: Bachelor thesis; not opened.
agent_relevance: Hint that narrowing the suspect scope is no gain unless the narrowing is correct.
